steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on estimating pixel-level uncertainty in deep learning models that segment landslides in satellite images. Motivate the problem (landslide hazards, incomplete databases, cost of labeling, human-in-the-loop curation), state the uncertainty methods we compare and how we evaluate them, give the main finding, and outline the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Landslide hazard and climate change
- Need for landslide databases; USGS database is incomplete
- Deep learning for landslide segmentation; single- vs multi-image tasks
- Manual labeling does not scale; semi-automated loop needs pixel-level confidence
- Three uncertainty methods compared; three evaluation measures; main result
- Paper organization

  - high-resolution satellite images increasingly available
  - recent efforts (cite): landslide segmentation (= landslide mapping), pixels that are landslide
  - labeling hard -> each study one small region, little test data; one study only 3 testing images (cite)
  - multi-image task: post-event + pre-event image pair; single-image task: one image, useful when no good pre-event image (cloud cover)
- Labeling and the curation loop
  - hard even for humans (Figure 1); landslides not salient; distractors like roads with similar color/texture
  - labelers needed training, compare to pre-event image; several minutes per image
  - semi-automated: train on initial data, segment more images, feed back, retrain

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Landslides are one of the most widespread hazards. 300M people are exposed to them and 66M people live in high-risk areas. Worldwide landslides cause thousands of deaths every year (\approx 4,164 in 2017 alone), and they also displace communities and destroy roads and habitable lands. On top of that, climate change is projected to cause more frequent extreme rainfalls and wildfires, and these are expected to lead to more landslides and more landslide-related casualties.

To mitigate the impacts of landslides in the long term, we need to evaluate landslide susceptibility. A large-scale database of satellite images of landslide events with accurate location information would help a lot with planning and prediction. In the US, the United States Geological Survey (USGS) keeps a database of landslide reports with approximate locations and times, but there are no images. And even this dataset, which is the most extensive of its kind, is incomplete and imprecise in location, since it only gives an approximate location. Each entry can be checked manually, either in person or by looking at satellite imagery, and this is both an opportunity and a challenge for scalability and coverage: “our current ability to understand landslide hazards at the national scale is limited, in part because spatial data on landslide occurrence across the U.S. varies greatly in quality, accessibility, and extent”.

High-resolution satellite images are becoming more available, so now it is possible to collect information about landslide events that are visible from space using satellite images. Several recent efforts have looked at using deep learning for landslide segmentation (also called landslide mapping), which means identifying the pixels in a satellite image that correspond to landslides. But because the training data is hard to label, each study focused on a single small region and had limited testing data (for example, one study only had 3 testing images).

There are two types of tasks. In the multi-image task, the input is a current image (post-event image) and an earlier image (pre-event image), and the goal is to identify the landslide in the post-event image, so it works with image pairs. In the single-image task there is just one image, and the goal is to identify the landslides in it, if there are any. This is useful when there are no high quality recent pre-event images (for example because of cloud cover).

Labeling training data by hand does not scale, because it is a hard problem even for humans (Figure 1 shows an example). Landslides are usually not the salient features in an image, and there are often “distractor” objects like roads that have similar color and texture. We found that for manual annotation we had to train the labelers, and they had to examine each satellite image carefully and compare it to the pre-event image. This takes a human annotator several minutes per image.

- Labeling and the curation loop
  - hard even for humans (Figure 1); landslides not salient; distractors like roads
  - labelers needed training, compare with pre-event image; several minutes per image
  - semi-automated loop; risk of propagating errors; human curators needed
  - key: pixel-level confidence; prioritize images; uncertainty contours suggest alternative segmentations
- Methods compared (no architecture change)
  - per-pixel scores thresholded; pre-threshold values as confidence, room for improvement
  - Pre-Threshold values: baseline, fastest
  - Monte-Carlo Dropout: models trained with dropout
  - TTA: average over rotated/flipped copies; approx. invariant; new in remote sensing
- Evaluation: calibration plots; AUC; best IOU over thresholds (image-specific thresholding)
- Result: TTA best on all three metrics across models
- Organization: Sections 3 to 8

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Landslides are one of the most widespread hazards. 300M people are exposed to them and 66M people live in high-risk areas. Worldwide landslides cause thousands of deaths every year (\approx 4,164 in 2017 alone), and they also displace communities and destroy roads and habitable lands. On top of that, climate change is projected to cause more frequent extreme rainfalls and wildfires, and these are expected to lead to more landslides and more landslide-related casualties.

To mitigate the impacts of landslides in the long term, we need to evaluate landslide susceptibility. A large-scale database of satellite images of landslide events with accurate location information would help a lot with planning and prediction. In the US, the United States Geological Survey (USGS) keeps a database of landslide reports with approximate locations and times, but there are no images. And even this dataset, which is the most extensive of its kind, is incomplete and imprecise in location, since it only gives an approximate location. Each entry can be checked manually, either in person or by looking at satellite imagery, and this is both an opportunity and a challenge for scalability and coverage: “our current ability to understand landslide hazards at the national scale is limited, in part because spatial data on landslide occurrence across the U.S. varies greatly in quality, accessibility, and extent”.

High-resolution satellite images are becoming more available, so now it is possible to collect information about landslide events that are visible from space using satellite images. Several recent efforts have looked at using deep learning for landslide segmentation (also called landslide mapping), which means identifying the pixels in a satellite image that correspond to landslides. But because the training data is hard to label, each study focused on a single small region and had limited testing data (for example, one study only had 3 testing images).

There are two types of tasks. In the multi-image task, the input is a current image (post-event image) and an earlier image (pre-event image), and the goal is to identify the landslide in the post-event image, so it works with image pairs. In the single-image task there is just one image, and the goal is to identify the landslides in it, if there are any. This is useful when there are no high quality recent pre-event images (for example because of cloud cover).

Labeling training data by hand does not scale, because it is a hard problem even for humans (Figure 1 shows an example). Landslides are usually not the salient features in an image, and there are often “distractor” objects like roads that have similar color and texture. We found that for manual annotation we had to train the labelers, and they had to examine each satellite image carefully and compare it to the pre-event image. This takes a human annotator several minutes per image.

Automated and semi-automated approaches for building landslide databases look more promising. One could take an initial dataset, train landslide segmentation models, and use them to segment more satellite images. These new images could then be added back to the training data, the models could be retrained, and so on. But if auto-segmented images are fed back into this training loop, there is a risk of propagating errors. Models trained on the new data will learn to make the same mistakes as the previous models, and maybe add new mistakes of their own. So human curators need to play a role in finding and correcting errors.

To make this kind of approach work, the key is to assess the pixel-level confidence of the segmentation models accurately, meaning for each pixel, how confident the model is that it is a landslide pixel. With accurate confidence estimates, curators can prioritize which images to check, and the contours of the uncertainty maps can be used to suggest alternative segmentations for an image (giving regions that can be added to or removed from an existing polygon).

Typical segmentation models give a score for every pixel. The scores are then thresholded, so values above the threshold are labeled as landslide and values below are labeled as background. In principle these pre-threshold values could be used as confidence measures, but in practice they can be improved a lot. In this paper we compare three methods for measuring per-pixel uncertainty, none of which change the underlying model architecture:

- Pre-Threshold values. These are a useful baseline and are the fastest to compute.

- Monte-Carlo Dropout. This method works for all models that are trained with dropout. Since dropout is a useful regularization technique, we count it as a training technique and not as a change to the architecture.

- Test-Time Augmentation (TTA). For a test image we make multiple augmented images (rotated, flipped, etc.). The confidence score of a pixel is the average of the pre-threshold values it gets from each of the augmented images. This makes the uncertainty scores robust, in the sense that they are now (approximately) invariant to augmentations. As far as we know, this technique has not been used before in the remote sensing domain.

We evaluate the confidence scores in three ways. (1) We make calibration plots, which show whether the confidence scores act like probabilities. For example, of all the pixels that have confidence 0.8 of being landslide, are 80% (or more) of them really landslide pixels? The other two measures look at how well the landslide confidence scores order the pixels. (2) Area Under the Curve (AUC) can be interpreted as the probability that a randomly chosen landslide pixel has a larger landslide-confidence score than a randomly chosen non-landslide pixel. (3) We also use an adaptation of AUC to typical segmentation metrics like Intersection Over Union (IOU). If we take the confidence map for an image and try all possible values of the threshold, what is the largest IOU we can get for the image? We call this image-specific thresholding.

We find that Test-Time Augmentation consistently does better than the other methods on all three metrics, across a variety of segmentation models.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 3 describes our landslide dataset. Our evaluation uses 4 standard deep learning architectures, and in Section 4 we explain what they are and briefly compare their accuracies. Section 5 describes the three techniques for generating confidence maps that we evaluate for each of the deep learning architectures. Section 6 describes our evaluation criteria. Section 7 has the results, and Section 8 gives conclusions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Landslides are one of the most widespread hazards, with 300M people exposed and 66M people in high-risk areas [1]. Globally, landslides cause thousands of deaths each year (\approx 4,164 in 2017 alone [2]), as well as the displacement of communities and the destruction of roads and habitable lands. Moreover, climate change is projected to induce more frequent extreme rainfalls and wildfires, which are expected to result in more landslides and landslide-related casualties [3,4].

Long-term efforts to mitigate the impacts of landslides require evaluating landslide susceptibility. Planning and prediction can be greatly assisted by a large-scale database of satellite images of landslide events with accurate location information. In the US, the United States Geological Survey (USGS) maintains a database of landslide reports with approximate locations and times (but no images). However, even this dataset, the most extensive of its kind, is incomplete and imprecise in location because it only gives an approximate location. While each entry can be verified manually, either in person or by examining satellite imagery, this presents both an opportunity and a challenge for scalability and coverage: “our current ability to understand landslide hazards at the national scale is limited, in part because spatial data on landslide occurrence across the U.S. varies greatly in quality, accessibility, and extent” [5].

Given the increasing availability of high-resolution satellite images, a path is now open to collect information about space-visible landslide events from satellite images. Several recent efforts [6,7] have considered deep learning for landslide segmentation (also known as landslide mapping), i.e. identifying the pixels in a satellite image that correspond to landslides. However, due to the difficulty of labeling training data, each study focused on a single small region and had limited testing data (for instance, one study only had 3 testing images [7]).

There are two types of tasks. The multi-image task takes a current (post-event) image and an earlier (pre-event) image, with the goal of identifying the landslide in the post-event image; it therefore deals with image pairs. The single-image task simply takes one image and identifies the landslides in it, if any exist. This is useful when high quality recent pre-event images are not available (for example, due to cloud cover).

Manually labeling training data does not scale, as it is a challenging problem even for humans (see Figure 1 for an example). Landslides are usually not the salient features in an image, and there are often “distractor” objects (like roads) with similar color and texture. We found that manual annotation required training the labelers, who had to carefully examine each satellite image and compare it to the pre-event image, a process that takes a human annotator several minutes per image.

Automated and semi-automated approaches for constructing landslide databases appear more promising: one could take an initial dataset, train landslide segmentation models and use them to segment additional satellite images. These new images could be fed back into the training data, models retrained, and so on. However, feeding auto-segmented images back into this training loop risks propagating errors, since models trained on the new data will learn to make the same mistakes as the previous models while possibly adding new mistakes of their own. Human curators must therefore play a role in detecting and correcting errors.

The key to making such an approach work is to accurately assess the pixel-level confidence of the segmentation models: for each pixel, how confident is the model that it is a landslide pixel? Accurate confidence estimates allow curators to prioritize the images they need to check, and contours of the uncertainty maps can suggest alternative segmentations for an image (providing regions that can be added to or removed from an existing polygon).

Typical segmentation models provide a score for every pixel. These scores are then thresholded: values above the threshold are labeled as landslide and values below as background. In principle, these pre-threshold values can serve as confidence measures, but in practice there is much room for improvement. In this paper, we compare three methods (none of which change the underlying model architecture) for measuring per-pixel uncertainty:

- Pre-Threshold values – a useful baseline that is computationally the fastest.

- Monte-Carlo Dropout [8] – applicable to all models trained with dropout [9] (since dropout is a useful regularization technique, we consider it a training technique rather than an architectural change).

- Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) [10] – for a test image, we prepare multiple augmented images (rotated, flipped, etc.), and a pixel's confidence score is the average of the pre-threshold values it receives from each augmented image. This makes the uncertainty scores robust in the sense that they are (approximately) invariant to augmentations. To the best of our knowledge, this technique has not been used before in the remote sensing domain.

We evaluate the confidence scores in three ways. (1) Calibration plots evaluate whether the confidence scores act like probabilities – e.g., of all pixels with confidence 0.8 of being landslide, are 80% (or more) of them actually landslide pixels? The next two measures evaluate how well the confidence scores order the pixels. (2) Area Under the Curve (AUC) can be interpreted as the probability that a randomly chosen landslide pixel has a larger landslide-confidence score than a randomly chosen non-landslide pixel. (3) We also consider an adaptation of AUC to typical segmentation metrics like Intersection Over Union (IOU): if we sweep out all possible threshold values on an image's confidence map, what is the largest IOU that can be achieved (which we call image-specific thresholding)?

We find that across a variety of segmentation models, Test-Time Augmentation consistently outperforms the other methods on all three metrics.

This paper is organized as follows. We describe our landslide dataset in Section 3. Our evaluation uses 4 standard deep learning architectures, which we explain and briefly compare in terms of accuracy in Section 4. In Section 5, we describe the three techniques for generating confidence maps that are evaluated for each architecture. Section 6 describes our evaluation criteria, results appear in Section 7, and we present conclusions in Section 8.
